title: Area and Perimeter Grade 4: The Formulas That Finally Make Sense + Free Quiz
meta_title: Area and Perimeter Grade 4: Formulas + Free Quiz
meta_desc: Master area and perimeter grade 4 with clear rectangle and square formulas, worked examples, missing-side tricks and a free 8-question quiz. Try it now.
excerpt: In Grade 3 your child counted squares. In Grade 4 they graduate to the formulas — and that is where a lot of children get area and perimeter tangled up. Here is how to keep them straight, with a free quiz to check.
author: Sachin Sharma
content:
Ask a Grade 4 class to find the perimeter of a rectangle and a good number will confidently multiply length by width — which is actually the area. Mixing up area and perimeter grade 4 style is the single most common slip I see, and it almost always traces back to one thing: the child learned two formulas but never really got what each one measures. So before a single number goes into a formula, get this straight — perimeter is the distance all the way around a shape, measured in plain units like cm; area is the flat surface it covers, measured in square units like cm². Same rectangle, two completely different questions.

Grade 3 was the counting-squares stage — drawing a grid inside a shape and counting the little boxes. That builds intuition, but it is slow and useless once the numbers get big. Grade 4 is the formula stage. The counting is behind us; now the job is to make the formulas feel obvious rather than magic.

The four formulas your child actually needs

There are only four, and two of them are just faster versions of the other two. Learn the rectangle pair first, then the square falls out for free because a square is simply a rectangle with all sides equal.

ShapePerimeterArea
Rectangle2 × (length + width)length × width
Square4 × sideside × side

Why 2 × (length + width) for the rectangle? Because a rectangle has two long sides and two short sides. Add one length and one width, then double it — you have gone all the way around. I always make children trace the outline with a finger while they say it. The physical loop of the finger is what makes ‘distance around’ stick.

A worked rectangle

Take a rectangle 8 cm long and 3 cm wide. Perimeter is 2 × (8 + 3) = 2 × 11 = 22 cm. Area is 8 × 3 = 24 cm². Notice the units: the perimeter answer is in cm, the area answer is in cm². If a child writes 24 cm for the area, the maths might be right but the answer is wrong — the unit is part of the answer at this stage, not an afterthought.

A worked square

A square tile has a side of 6 cm. Perimeter is 4 × 6 = 24 cm. Area is 6 × 6 = 36 cm². Point out that even though both come from the number 6, one adds up four equal sides and the other covers a surface — different jobs, different units.

Keeping area and perimeter apart

Here is the trick that has saved more of my students than any other. Tie each word to a real picture:

  • Perimeter — think of a fence around a garden, or the frame around a photo. You are walking the edge. Answer in cm, m, or km.
  • Area — think of the grass inside the fence, or the tiles covering a floor. You are filling the inside. Answer in square units: cm², m².

One counter-intuitive fact worth showing a curious child: two rectangles can have the same perimeter but wildly different areas. A 1 × 9 rectangle and a 5 × 5 square both have a perimeter of 20, but their areas are 9 and 25. That single example does more to separate the two ideas than a page of definitions.

Finding a missing side

This is the Grade 4 skill that separates children who memorised formulas from children who understand them. Sometimes you are given the area or perimeter and asked to work backwards to a side.

Say a rectangle has an area of 24 cm² and a length of 6 cm. Since area = length × width, we need the number that multiplies with 6 to make 24. That is 24 ÷ 6 = 4 cm. Division undoes the multiplication.

Perimeter works the same way in reverse. If a square has a perimeter of 20 cm, and perimeter = 4 × side, then side = 20 ÷ 4 = 5 cm. Teach it as ‘whatever the formula does, undo it’ — multiply becomes divide, and add becomes subtract.

Simple L-shaped figures

Once rectangles are solid, Grade 4 introduces compound shapes — usually an L made of two rectangles stuck together. Do not panic children with a new formula, because there isn’t one. The method is: split the L into two plain rectangles, find the area of each, and add them.

For perimeter of an L-shape, the honest approach at Grade 4 is to add up every outside edge, one at a time, all the way around. It is slower, but it keeps the meaning of perimeter — distance around — front and centre, which matters more than a shortcut here.

A realistic practice plan

Ten focused minutes beats a marathon session. What has worked for parents I know in Tier-2 cities where tutoring is not always an option: two days on rectangle formulas, two days on squares and mixed problems, one day on missing sides, and the weekend on one or two L-shapes plus a quick mixed quiz. The key is mixing area and perimeter questions together so the child has to decide which formula fits — that deciding step is where real understanding lives. One honest caveat: do not rush to word problems until the plain formulas are automatic, or the child ends up guessing.

Test what your child has learned

Below is a free 8-question quiz covering exactly these ideas — rectangle and square formulas, the area-versus-perimeter difference, missing sides, and a simple compound shape. Let your child try it and read the explanations together for anything they miss. When they are ready for longer written practice, the printable worksheet at the end has graded questions with a full answer key.

quiz.title: Grade 4 Area and Perimeter Quiz
quiz.intro: Eight quick questions on rectangle and square formulas, the area-versus-perimeter difference, missing sides and an L-shape. Pick an answer for each, then press Check my score.
quiz.about: Grade 4 area and perimeter using formulas

questions.q: What is the perimeter of a rectangle 7 cm long and 4 cm wide?
What is the area of a rectangle 7 cm long and 4 cm wide?
questions.explanation: Area = length × width = 7 × 4 = 28 cm². Notice the answer is in square units.

questions.q: What is the perimeter of a square with side 9 cm?
questions.explanation: Perimeter of a square = 4 × side = 4 × 9 = 36 cm.

questions.q: What is the area of a square with side 5 cm?
questions.explanation: Area of a square = side × side = 5 × 5 = 25 cm².

options: The distance all the way around a shape
questions.explanation: Perimeter is the distance around the outside, measured in plain units like cm. Area is the surface covered, in square units.

questions.q: A rectangle has an area of 30 cm² and a length of 6 cm. What is its width?
questions.explanation: Area = length × width, so width = area ÷ length = 30 ÷ 6 = 5 cm. Division undoes the multiplication.

questions.q: A square has a perimeter of 32 cm. What is the length of one side?
An L-shape is made of two rectangles, one of area 12 cm² and one of area 8 cm². What is the total area?
questions.explanation: Split the L into two rectangles and add their areas: 12 + 8 = 20 cm².

faq.q: What is the difference between area and perimeter in Grade 4?
faq.a: Perimeter is the distance all the way around a shape, measured in plain units like cm. Area is the flat surface the shape covers, measured in square units like cm². Same shape, two different questions — and two different units.

faq.q: What are the area and perimeter formulas a Grade 4 student should know?
faq.a: Four formulas: rectangle perimeter is 2 × (length + width) and rectangle area is length × width; square perimeter is 4 × side and square area is side × side. Learn the rectangle pair first, and the square follows because a square is a rectangle with equal sides.

faq.q: How do you find a missing side when the area or perimeter is given?
faq.a: Work backwards with division. If a rectangle’s area is 24 cm² and its length is 6 cm, the width is 24 ÷ 6 = 4 cm. If a square’s perimeter is 20 cm, one side is 20 ÷ 4 = 5 cm. Whatever the formula multiplies, you divide to undo it.

faq.q: How do you find the area of an L-shaped figure?
faq.a: Split the L into two plain rectangles, find the area of each with length × width, then add the two areas together. There is no separate L-shape formula at Grade 4.
